## Discrete-time models — Day 1, Session 4

Worksheet: `worksheets/04-discrete-time-models.qmd`. The chapter is
[Discrete-time models](../chapters/02-discrete-time-models.qmd).

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch02-setup
using Distributions
using StableRNGs
using Statistics
using CairoMakie

check(name, condition) =
    println(condition ? "✓ $name" : "✗ $name — not right yet, see the hint")

rate_to_proportion(r, δt) = -expm1(-r * δt)

function sir_map_step(state, p, δt)
    S, I, R = state
    infection = rate_to_proportion(p.β * p.c * I / p.N, δt) * S
    recovery  = rate_to_proportion(p.γ, δt) * I
    return (S - infection, I + infection - recovery, R + recovery)
end

function iterate_model(step, u0, p, δt, nsteps; extra = ())
    traj = Matrix{Float64}(undef, 3, nsteps + 1)
    traj[:, 1] .= u0
    state = Tuple(float.(u0))
    for k in 1:nsteps
        state = step(state, p, δt, extra...)
        traj[:, k + 1] .= state
    end
    return traj
end

u0     = [990, 10, 0]
p      = (β = 0.05, c = 10.0, γ = 0.25, N = 1000.0, ω = 0.02)
δt     = 1.0
nsteps = 728          # two years, and exactly 104 whole weeks
ts     = 0:nsteps

sir_traj = iterate_model((s, p, dt) -> sir_map_step(s, p, dt), u0, p, δt, nsteps)

println("R₀ = ", p.β * p.c / p.γ)
println("peak infectious: ", round(maximum(sir_traj[2, :]), digits = 1))
println("infectious at two years: ", round(sir_traj[2, end], digits = 1))
```

### Part A — immunity that does not last

The third transition needs one new line and two changed terms. `waning` is a
number of people, exactly like `infection` and `recovery`: the conversion turns
the rate `p.ω` into a per-step proportion, and multiplying by `R` turns that
proportion into a count.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch02-a1
function sirs_map_step(state, p, δt)
    S, I, R = state
    infection = rate_to_proportion(p.β * p.c * I / p.N, δt) * S
    recovery  = rate_to_proportion(p.γ, δt) * I
    waning    = rate_to_proportion(p.ω, δt) * R
    return (S - infection + waning, I + infection - recovery, R + recovery - waning)
end

sirs_traj = iterate_model((s, p, dt) -> sirs_map_step(s, p, dt), u0, p, δt, nsteps)

# What the continuous-time theory predicts for the endemic state.
R₀ = p.β * p.c / p.γ
S_endemic = p.N / R₀
I_endemic = p.N * (1 - 1 / R₀) / (1 + p.γ / p.ω)

check("population still conserved",
      all(k -> isapprox(sum(sirs_traj[:, k]), p.N; atol = 1e-8), 1:nsteps+1))
check("immunity is waning", sirs_traj[1, end] > 300)
check("the disease is still circulating after two years", sirs_traj[2, end] > 10)
check("the model has settled down",
      abs(sirs_traj[2, end] - sirs_traj[2, end-28]) < 0.01 * sirs_traj[2, end])
check("prevalence lands within 30% of the analytic endemic level",
      isapprox(sirs_traj[2, end], I_endemic; rtol = 0.3))

(; S_at_two_years = round(sirs_traj[1, end]; digits = 1),
   I_at_two_years = round(sirs_traj[2, end]; digits = 1),
   S_endemic = round(S_endemic; digits = 1),
   I_endemic = round(I_endemic; digits = 1))
```

The endemic values come from setting all three continuous flows to zero:

$$
\frac{S^\ast}{N} = \frac{1}{R_0}, \qquad
I^\ast = N\,\frac{1 - 1/R_0}{1 + \gamma/\omega},
$$

which for the baseline with $\omega = 0.02$ gives $S^\ast = 500$ and
$I^\ast \approx 37$. Note that $S^\ast$ depends only on $R_0$: the waning rate
sets how many people are infectious, not how many are susceptible.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ws-ch02-endemic
#| fig-cap: "Infectious compartment over two years under the deterministic map, with and without waning immunity. The dotted line is the endemic level predicted by continuous-time theory."
fig = Figure(size = (720, 400))
ax  = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "time (days)", ylabel = "infectious I(t)",
           title = "One outbreak, or a disease that stays")
lines!(ax, ts, sir_traj[2, :]; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 3,
       label = "no waning (SIR)")
lines!(ax, ts, sirs_traj[2, :]; color = :steelblue, linewidth = 3,
       label = "waning immunity (SIRS)")
hlines!(ax, [I_endemic]; color = :black, linestyle = :dot,
        label = "analytic endemic level")
axislegend(ax; position = :rt)
fig
```

#### A1. Interpret

- With waning the first wave peaks at 209 on day 19, against 201 on day 18
  without it. Prevalence then falls to a trough of 19.3 on day 60, rises to a
  smaller second wave of about 61 around day 107, and settles at 45 infectious
  with 447 susceptible.
- The early epidemic is almost unchanged because the waning flow is $\omega R_t$
  and $R_t$ starts at zero: for the first fortnight there is nobody to lose
  immunity, and the two curves stay within 1% of each other through day 13.
- What ends that is the size of $R_t$, not the passage of time. Once the wave has
  built a recovered pool, the gap opens fast — 5% by day 20, 10% by day 24 —
  enough to lift the peak from 201 to 209 and push it a day later. "No difference
  early" is an approximation, and $R_t$ is what marks when it stops holding.
- The trough refills with susceptibles. The wave ends because $S$ fell below
  $N/R_0$, not because the pathogen went anywhere, and immunity keeps expiring at
  rate $\omega R$ while prevalence is low. Once $S$ climbs back above the
  threshold transmission grows again, giving the second wave and a damped
  oscillation towards the endemic level rather than a smooth approach.
- The plateau sits above the analytic line because of the step size. Both flows
  use $1 - e^{-r\delta t}$, which understates $r\delta t$ more when $r\delta t$ is
  larger: recovery has $\gamma\delta t = 0.25$ and is throttled by 11.5% (0.2212
  instead of 0.25), while infection has $\beta c I \delta t / N \approx 0.023$ and
  is throttled by only 1.1%.
- Per step the map therefore recovers people relatively more slowly than it
  infects them, so the balance point moves to fewer susceptibles and more
  infectious. This is a property of $\delta t = 1$ day, not of the model: the step
  is a quarter of the 4-day infectious period, while the 50-day immunity is finely
  resolved by comparison.

#### A2. Refine the step

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch02-a2
runs = map([1.0, 0.5, 0.1]) do dt
    n = round(Int, nsteps / dt)
    traj = iterate_model((s, p, d) -> sirs_map_step(s, p, d), u0, p, dt, n)
    (δt = dt, traj = traj)
end

refinement = [(δt = r.δt, S = round(r.traj[1, end]; digits = 1),
               I = round(r.traj[2, end]; digits = 1)) for r in runs]

fine = last(runs).traj      # the δt = 0.1 run

check("the refined map lands on the analytic susceptible level",
      isapprox(fine[1, end] / p.N, 1 / R₀; atol = 0.01))
check("the one-day step is several percent away from it",
      abs(sirs_traj[1, end] / p.N - 1 / R₀) > 0.03)

refinement
```

- The endemic state moves from $(S, I) = (447.4, 45.4)$ at $\delta t = 1$, to
  $(472.4, 41.2)$ at $\delta t = 0.5$, to $(494.3, 37.9)$ at $\delta t = 0.1$.
  Halving the step roughly halves the gap to the analytic $(500, 37.0)$ — the
  first-order convergence the session measured against the ODE, seen here in an
  equilibrium instead of at a fixed time.
- At $\delta t = 1$ day the discretisation error in reported prevalence is about
  23%. That is probably smaller than the uncertainty in $\omega$, since "immunity
  lasts 50 days" is a guess to within a factor of two — but the two are not
  equivalent. Parameter uncertainty is a fact about the world; this bias is a
  choice, it costs nothing to remove, and nothing in the output announces it.
- It grows quickly. A weekly step, $\delta t = 7$, tempting when the data are
  weekly, lands on $(S, I) = (279, 98)$, nowhere near the continuous-time model
  it is meant to approximate.
- The step width is a numerical decision rather than a reporting one. Weekly data
  is a reason to aggregate a finely-stepped model up to weeks, as in Part C,
  rather than to step it weekly.

### Part B — the same model with integer people

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch02-b1
function sirs_chain_step(state, p, δt, rng)
    S, I, R = state
    Y = rand(rng, Binomial(round(Int, S), rate_to_proportion(p.β * p.c * I / p.N, δt)))
    Z = rand(rng, Binomial(round(Int, I), rate_to_proportion(p.γ, δt)))
    W = rand(rng, Binomial(round(Int, R), rate_to_proportion(p.ω, δt)))
    return (S - Y + W, I + Y - Z, R + Z - W)
end

nsims = 100
chain_ens = [iterate_model(sirs_chain_step, u0, p, δt, nsteps; extra = (StableRNG(seed),))
             for seed in 1:nsims]
chain_I = reduce(hcat, (traj[2, :] for traj in chain_ens))
chain_mean_I = vec(mean(chain_I; dims = 2))

died_out = [any(iszero, traj[2, :]) for traj in chain_ens]

check("every realisation conserves the population",
      all(traj -> all(k -> sum(traj[:, k]) == p.N, 1:nsteps+1), chain_ens))
check("and every compartment stays a whole number",
      all(traj -> all(isinteger, traj), chain_ens))
check("some realisations faded out", count(died_out) >= 3)
check("but not all of them", 0 < count(died_out) < nsims)
check("the ensemble mean tracks the map through the first wave",
      isapprox(maximum(chain_mean_I[1:80]), maximum(sirs_traj[2, 1:80]); rtol = 0.1))

(; fade_out_fraction = count(died_out) / nsims,
   chain_mean_at_two_years = round(chain_mean_I[end]; digits = 1),
   map_at_two_years = round(sirs_traj[2, end]; digits = 1))
```

`any(iszero, traj[2, :])` is the whole test: it asks whether the infectious
compartment was ever zero. `traj[2, end] == 0` returns the same count here,
because $I = 0$ is absorbing and nothing can reintroduce the disease. The two
part company as soon as a model gains importation or a second coupled
population, and only the first still answers "did this disease ever go extinct".

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch02-b1-extra
extinction_days = sort([findfirst(iszero, traj[2, :]) - 1
                        for traj in chain_ens if any(iszero, traj[2, :])])
survivors = [traj for traj in chain_ens if !any(iszero, traj[2, :])]

(; extinction_days,
   survivor_mean_at_two_years = round(mean(traj[2, end] for traj in survivors); digits = 1),
   map_at_two_years = round(sirs_traj[2, end]; digits = 1))
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ws-ch02-chain
#| fig-cap: "One hundred stochastic SIRS realisations (thin grey), their ensemble mean (red), and the deterministic map (dashed black). Runs that reach zero infectious stay there."
fig2 = Figure(size = (720, 440))
ax2  = Axis(fig2[1, 1]; xlabel = "time (days)", ylabel = "infectious I(t)",
            title = "Persisting in most runs, faded out in some")
for j in 1:nsims
    lines!(ax2, ts, chain_I[:, j]; color = (:grey, 0.15), linewidth = 1)
end
lines!(ax2, ts, chain_mean_I; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 3, label = "chain mean")
lines!(ax2, ts, sirs_traj[2, :]; color = :black, linestyle = :dash, linewidth = 3,
       label = "deterministic map")
axislegend(ax2; position = :rt)
fig2
```

#### B1. Interpret

- Eight of the 100 realisations died out, seven between days 57 and 101 and one
  straggler on day 685.
- That window is the trough. The first wave overshoots, driving $S$ well below
  the threshold, so prevalence collapses to a handful of cases — around 19 in the
  map and lower in many realisations. With that few, a short run of chance
  recoveries and no new infections wipes the disease out, and nothing brings it
  back. By the time waning has lifted prevalence to 40-odd cases, extinction needs
  a far longer unlucky streak.
- The mean does not describe a typical realisation. At two years it is 40.9
  against the map's 45.4, and most of that gap is the eight dead runs averaged in
  as zeros: the survivors average 44.5, within 2% of the map.
- Even setting extinctions aside, there is no reason the survivors should land on
  the map. The map is the chain's expectation for *one step from a given state*,
  and the infection update is nonlinear, so iterating the map is a mean-field
  approximation of the ensemble mean, not the mean itself.
- These 100 runs cannot show that. The survivors sit 0.9 below the map with a
  standard error of about 2, so a systematic gap is indistinguishable from
  sampling noise; 2000 runs would bring the standard error to 0.4 and resolve a
  gap of roughly one infectious person. What an ensemble can resolve sets the
  size of difference worth reading anything into.
- The distribution is bimodal — faded out, or persisting near the endemic level —
  and the mean sits in a gap where no realisation lives, which is what averaging
  a bimodal outcome generally does. An absorbing state is the common way a model
  acquires one.
- Only the chain can say whether the disease is still here in five years, and it
  answers a narrower question than the map appears to. The map moves fractions of
  people, so $I_t$ decays towards zero without arriving: extinction is a question
  its state space cannot represent, and its "endemic equilibrium" is permanent.
- The chain has no permanent endemic state to offer in exchange. $I = 0$ is
  reachable from any state and nothing brings the disease back, so every
  realisation ends at zero if you wait long enough. What the chain gives is a
  *probability over a horizon*: 92 of 100 runs still had the disease at two years,
  and five years would give a fraction no larger.
- The figure shows one further difference. The map's oscillation damps out to a
  flat line, while individual realisations keep fluctuating around the endemic
  level for the full two years, some still touching 168 cases more than a year
  after the wave. Randomness does not merely blur the deterministic answer: it
  keeps re-exciting the oscillation the map settles out of, so a real endemic
  disease shows recurrent epidemics where the map shows a plateau.

#### B2. Experiment

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch02-b2
function fade_out_fraction(N, trials)
    p_N  = merge(p, (N = Float64(N),))
    u0_N = [N - 10, 10, 0]
    runs = (iterate_model(sirs_chain_step, u0_N, p_N, δt, nsteps;
                          extra = (StableRNG(1000 + k),)) for k in 1:trials)
    return count(traj -> any(iszero, traj[2, :]), runs) / trials
end

populations = [200, 1000, 5000]

fractions = [fade_out_fraction(N, 50) for N in populations]
for (N, f) in zip(populations, fractions)
    println("N = $N → the disease died out in $(round(100f; digits = 0))% of runs")
end

check("three population sizes tried", length(populations) == 3)
check("fade-out becomes rarer as the population grows", issorted(fractions; rev = true))
```

- Within the two-year horizon the disease faded out in 100% of runs at $N = 200$,
  8% at $N = 1000$, and none at all at $N = 5000$, with $R_0 = 2$ throughout.
- Endemic prevalence is a fixed *fraction* of the population, so the trough after
  the first wave scales with $N$: about 4 infectious people in a community of 200,
  around 19 in 1000, roughly 95 in 5000. Fade-out needs the trough to reach zero
  by chance, which becomes very unlikely once it holds tens of cases.
- This is the idea of a **critical community size**. It is a probabilistic scale
  rather than a hard threshold: there is no population below which persistence is
  impossible and above which it is guaranteed, and the scale shifts with
  transmission, recovery, waning and importation.
- All three populations would lose the disease eventually, since nothing here
  reintroduces it. $N$ changes how long that takes, not whether it happens.
- For an elimination target, $R_0$ is therefore not enough on its own. A small
  community keeps losing the disease by luck and keeps having it reintroduced, so
  national persistence depends on population size and connectivity as well as the
  local reproduction number. This model cannot speak to connectivity — one closed,
  well-mixed population, no importation — which is what the model-composition
  material in the appendices builds.

### Part C — from prevalence to incident infections

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch02-c1
function iterate_with_incidence(u0, p, δt, nsteps)
    traj = Matrix{Float64}(undef, 3, nsteps + 1)
    incidence = Vector{Float64}(undef, nsteps)
    state = Tuple(float.(u0))
    traj[:, 1] .= u0
    for k in 1:nsteps
        S, I, R = state
        incidence[k] = rate_to_proportion(p.β * p.c * I / p.N, δt) * S
        state = sirs_map_step(state, p, δt)
        traj[:, k + 1] .= state
    end
    return traj, incidence
end

traj_c, daily_cases = iterate_with_incidence(u0, p, δt, nsteps)

nweeks = div(nsteps, 7)
weekly_cases = Float64[]

for w in 1:nweeks
    week = daily_cases[(7 * (w - 1) + 1):(7 * w)]   # the seven daily numbers of week w
    push!(weekly_cases, sum(week))
end

check("one total per week, and every week has cases in it",
      length(weekly_cases) == nweeks && all(>(0), weekly_cases))
check("no cases lost in the aggregation",
      isapprox(sum(weekly_cases), sum(daily_cases); rtol = 1e-10))
check("incidence peaks before prevalence", argmax(daily_cases) < argmax(traj_c[2, :]))

(; total_cases = round(sum(daily_cases); digits = 0),
   cases_per_person = round(sum(daily_cases) / p.N; digits = 1),
   incidence_peak_day = argmax(daily_cases) - 1,
   prevalence_peak_day = argmax(traj_c[2, :]) - 1)
```

- The incidence recorded is the `infection` term the step already computes, the
  flow $S \to I$, captured before the state is updated so that it uses the same
  $S$ and $I$ the step used. Nothing new is calculated; a quantity that was
  discarded is kept.
- Cases are counts, so a week's total is the sum of its seven days. The loop above
  is the explicit version; as a comprehension it would more often be written
  `weekly_cases = [sum(daily_cases[(7 * (w - 1) + 1):(7 * w)]) for w in 1:nweeks]`.
- This works only because incidence is a flow. Aggregating a *prevalence* series
  the same way would be meaningless, since Monday's infectious people and
  Tuesday's are largely the same people.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch02-c1-extra
(; peak_week = argmax(weekly_cases),
   peak_week_cases = round(maximum(weekly_cases); digits = 0),
   first_eight_weeks = round(sum(weekly_cases[1:8]); digits = 0),
   remaining_96_weeks = round(sum(weekly_cases[9:end]); digits = 0),
   endemic_weekly = round(mean(weekly_cases[80:end]); digits = 1))
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ws-ch02-reporting
#| fig-cap: "Top: daily incident infections and prevalence over the first wave. Each incidence value covers a one-day interval and is labelled by the day that interval starts; prevalence is an instantaneous state read at each day. The busiest incidence interval starts on day 15 and prevalence peaks at day 19, so incidence turns over earlier. Bottom: the same epidemic as 104 weekly infection totals, the shape a case series arrives in."
fig3 = Figure(size = (720, 600))

ax3 = Axis(fig3[1, 1]; xlabel = "time (days)", ylabel = "people",
           title = "New infections lead prevalence")
lines!(ax3, 0:120, traj_c[2, 1:121]; color = :steelblue, linewidth = 3,
       label = "prevalence I(t)")
lines!(ax3, 0:119, daily_cases[1:120]; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 3,
       label = "new infections per day")
vlines!(ax3, [argmax(daily_cases) - 1]; color = :firebrick, linestyle = :dot)
vlines!(ax3, [argmax(traj_c[2, :]) - 1]; color = :steelblue, linestyle = :dot)
axislegend(ax3; position = :rt)

ax4 = Axis(fig3[2, 1]; xlabel = "week", ylabel = "incident infections",
           title = "Two years of weekly totals")
barplot!(ax4, 1:nweeks, weekly_cases; color = :seagreen, gap = 0.1)

fig3
```

#### C1. Interpret

- The busiest daily interval starts on day 15, with about 53 new infections;
  prevalence peaks four days later, on day 19, at about 209. Weekly totals peak in
  week 3 with 338 infections and settle at about 70 a week.
- Surveillance follows incidence. Routine notification counts events as they are
  reported, so it tracks the flow of new cases rather than how many are infectious
  at that moment.
- What the model gives here is *infections*, which match notifications only if
  every case is detected and reported straight away. With reporting delays and
  incomplete detection the observed peak arrives later and flatter, and the
  observation-model session adds exactly those effects.
- Prevalence is not unobservable, but it needs a different instrument: a
  representative survey, sentinel sampling, or a register of people currently
  infected.
- The two peaks are different events. Incidence peaks when the shrinking
  susceptible pool starts to outweigh the growing infectious pool; prevalence
  peaks later, when inflow falls to meet outflow — at day 19 there are 43 new
  infections against 46 recoveries. Comparing a model's prevalence peak with a
  notified-case peak puts the turning point about four days late, which matters
  when the question is whether an epidemic has turned this week.
- The 7.7 infections per person is $\omega$ doing the work. With immunity lasting
  a mean of 50 days a person can be reinfected every couple of months, so over two
  years the model delivers about eight infections each and cumulative incidence
  far exceeds the population. Fifty days is short for most infections — plausible
  for some respiratory and enteric pathogens, wildly wrong for measles — so the
  parameter is the questionable part, not the arithmetic. With $\omega$ near zero
  the model collapses back to Part A's single wave.
- The epidemic is not over, and the weekly totals make that case better than any
  prevalence curve: the visible epidemic, the first eight weeks, produced about
  1040 infections, while the 96 quiet weeks that follow produced about 6700. A
  disease that has stopped making headlines can carry most of its burden
  afterwards, spread thinly, and a surveillance series is what makes that visible.
